source: Kimball & Metcalfe (2003) Delaying judgments of learning affects memory, not metamemory
finding: Standard delayed-JOL effect reproduced when targets are not re-shown. When the target is re-shown right after the JOL, the effect vanishes. This supports the memory hypothesis: covert retrieval at the JOL helps memory, so retrieved items get high JOLs and high recall.
numbers: Exp 3 (N=40): no reexposure, delayed cue-only gamma .76 vs immediate cue-only .36 (F(1,35)=24.29, p<.0001). With reexposure: .53 vs .43, n.s. Exp 2 (N=72): unreexposed delayed cue-only .72 vs cue-target .43 (p=.0024); reexposed .39 vs .46, n.s.
quote: Metamemory theories claim that memory monitoring improves under these conditions.
limits: Word pairs only. Gamma is a ranking statistic. The result shows the JOL procedure changes memory; it does not prove monitoring never improves.
agent_relevance: Part of a delayed monitoring signal is a memory event. A retrieval attempt before a confidence call both gives information and changes the outcome.

source: Kimball & Metcalfe (2003) Exp 1 (cue-only vs cue-target delayed JOLs)
finding: In Exp 1 the usual advantage of cue-only over cue-target delayed JOLs did not appear when all targets were re-shown after the JOL.
numbers: N=36 undergraduates, 84 pairs. Delayed cue-only gamma M=.52 (SE .07) vs delayed cue-target M=.41 (SE .06), t(34)=1.16, p>.25.
limits: Single lab, one stimulus set. Contrasts with the gap reported by Dunlosky and Nelson (1992, 1997).
agent_relevance: A boundary condition: monitoring accuracy depends on what the system can still retrieve unaided at judgment time.

source: Kimball & Metcalfe (2003) recall by JOL level
finding: Low-JOL items that were neither retrieved nor re-shown were recalled worst. That drop, not better insight, produced the high delayed gamma.
numbers: Exp 2 three-way interaction of JOL format x JOL level x reexposure: F(1,64)=10.60, p=.0018.
limits: Analysis grouped JOL levels (lowest 3 vs highest 4) and dropped participants who did not use both groups.
agent_relevance: If the agent attempts retrieval before judging, its confidence tracks retrieval success. Re-reading the answer first destroys the signal.

source: Maki (1998) Predicting performance on text: delayed versus immediate predictions and tests
finding: The delayed-JOL advantage found for word pairs did not carry over to text. Immediate predictions with an immediate test were best. Delayed predictions did not beat immediate ones when the test was delayed.
numbers: N=96 (4 groups of 24); prediction gamma differed by group, F(3,92)=3.34. Only the immediate-prediction/immediate-test group had prediction gamma reliably above zero.
quote: The results for delayed judgments of learning with text were different from those with word pairs.
limits: Texts with multiple-choice questions. Per-group gamma values are in figures. Read from the PDF text.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition for a gate on complex tasks: the near-perfect delayed accuracy seen with pairs does not generalise to rich materials.

source: Maki (1998) posttest confidence vs prediction
finding: Confidence given after answering test questions was accurate in every condition. Predictions made before the test were not (except the immediate/immediate case).
numbers: Posttest confidence gamma above zero in all conditions; prediction gamma not different from zero in the immediate-prediction/delayed-test group and both delayed-prediction groups; posttest confidence ANOVA F<1.
limits: Same single study.
agent_relevance: Judging after attempting is more reliable than predicting before. This favours a cheap probe attempt over a pure up-front prediction at S0.

source: Tekin & Roediger (2021) Metacognition and Learning 16:407-429, delayed JOLs and retention
finding: Tested whether delayed JOLs themselves boost later recall. The effect was small and unstable: present in one within-subject experiment, absent in a direct online replication.
numbers: Exp 1 N=164: recall restudy .44, cue-target JOL .45, cue-only JOL .50, overt retrieval .52 (cue-only vs restudy d=.38, p=.264). Exp 2a N=53: JOL-only d=.63 vs restudy. Exp 2b N=41 replication: JOL-only vs restudy diff .02, d=.11, p=.90.
limits: Exp 1 underpowered (min detectable f=.23). Page read to 100,000 of 105,193 characters. Effect seems to depend on covert retrieval: Exp 2a 'yes' items recalled .71 vs .34 for 'no'.
agent_relevance: The retrieval-practice side effect of a judgment is real but weak. Judgment steps should not be counted on as free learning.

source: Rhodes & Tauber (2011) meta-analysis of delayed JOLs (as reported in Tekin & Roediger 2021)
finding: Across 98 effect sizes, delayed JOLs beat immediate JOLs only modestly overall, and mostly with the cue-target format. Cue-only format gave almost no benefit.
numbers: As cited by Tekin & Roediger: overall g=0.08; cue-target JOLs g=0.70; cue-only g=0.03. I read the secondary citation, not the 2011 paper.
limits: Secondary report. Exact metric is as quoted by the citing paper; check the original before relying on it.
agent_relevance: The meta-analytic gain from delaying is far smaller than the famous near-perfect gamma values suggest.

source: Nelson & Dunlosky (1991) The delayed-JOL effect (founding study, search snippet only)
finding: Delayed JOLs for word pairs predicted later recall almost perfectly; immediate JOLs much less. Named the delayed-JOL effect.
numbers: Snippet only: gamma 'nearly perfect' for delayed JOLs. Second-hand gammas in Kimball & Metcalfe are .72-.76 for delayed cue-only.
limits: Not opened. Sample sizes and delays unverified.
agent_relevance: The founding result that later work qualifies.

source: Weaver & Kelemen (1997) Judgments of learning at delays (search snippet only)
finding: Part of the delayed-JOL advantage may come from a shift in how scale values are used. Delayed JOLs used scale ends more. Simulations suggested most of the effect was still real calibration.
numbers: Snippet: over 50 percent of delayed judgments used scale ends; immediate judgments clustered mid-scale.
limits: Not opened. Details from a search summary.
agent_relevance: Response-style artifacts can inflate a metacognitive accuracy measure.

source: Spellman, Bloomfield & Bjork (2008) on gamma as a measure (search snippet only)
finding: Gamma has statistical problems for judging metamemory. A person with perfect knowledge of initial learning will not generally get gamma of 1.
numbers: Snippet only. Download failed, not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Use discrimination measures with known properties (AUROC, Brier) when scoring our agent's confidence, not gamma alone.

source: Koriat (2026) Confidence judgments, feelings of knowing and judgments of learning: towards a common framework (Mem Cognit)
finding: Argues FOK and JOL, like confidence, reflect how consistent the cues are that are sampled for that item. Judgments agree across people because they share the same knowledge pool.
numbers: FOK study (90 items, 36 people): consensual choices stronger, M=91.2 vs 85.1, t(35)=8.91. JOL study (58 items, 24 people): 78.67 vs 62.99, t(23)=9.27. Replicability r=.47 for high-association JOL pairs; r=.04 for unrelated pairs.
quote: consistency of item-specific cues randomly sampled from a 'collective wisdomware' pool
limits: Re-analyses of published small single-lab data. Effects absent for unrelated JOL pairs. FOK is about recognition, JOL about recall.
agent_relevance: Item-level difficulty feelings are partly shared, hence predictable. Agreement across several samples is a candidate difficulty signal.

source: Koriat (2026) FOK vs JOL differences
finding: FOK runs higher than JOL, and the consensuality slope is steeper for JOLs. The article gives no explanation for that interaction.
numbers: Mean FOK 89.8 vs JOL 74.7. Consensuality slope b=6.06 (JOL) vs 3.48 (FOK). Children grades 1-6 showed the same pattern; between-individual replicability r=.44 overall, r=.30 in grade 1.
limits: Page read to 100,000 of 124,443 characters. Different binary cutoffs used (63 for FOK, 50 for JOL).
agent_relevance: Judgment type matters: an up-front 'will I learn this' call and a post-failure 'do I know this' call are not the same signal.

source: Pournaghdali, Schwartz & Soto (2025) Tip-of-the-tongue and feeling-of-knowing enhance metacognitive sensitivity (J Cogn)
finding: After a recall failure, confidence in a later recognition answer was at chance when no TOT or only a low FOK was present. Sensitivity rose above chance as TOT or FOK got stronger.
numbers: Exp 1 faces N=70 analysed (76 recruited); Exp 2 general knowledge N=47 (64 recruited). Exp1 TOT M=3.08 vs 1.48, chi2(1)=72; Exp2 TOT 2.90 vs 1.76, chi2(1)=47.1. No meta-d' or AUC values reported.
limits: Not preregistered. Binary TOT/FOK scales. Mostly female sample in Exp 1 (64 of 70). Page read to 100,000 of 131,838 characters.
agent_relevance: A missing feeling of partial access carries little information; the feeling itself adds signal.

source: Ingendahl & Undorf (2026) Instructed learning strategy use eliminates negative reactivity of immediate JOLs (Psychon Bull Rev)
finding: Making immediate JOLs lowers later recall of unrelated pairs and raises recall of related pairs. Telling learners to use a strategy on unrelated pairs removes both effects.
numbers: Preregistered. Exp 1 N=193: related d=0.43, unrelated d=0.80 (negative). Exp 2 N=200: related d=0.38, unrelated d=0.41. Imagery instruction raised unrelated recall vs plain JOL by d=1.15 (Exp 1), d=0.54 (Exp 2).
limits: German students, cued recall only. Mediation exploratory. Authors cite a meta-analysis with smaller negative effects and publication bias.
agent_relevance: Prompting for a judgment can change task performance, and an explicit strategy cue removes the cost. Judgment steps need a strategy instruction attached.

source: Ingendahl & Undorf (2026) Are restudy decisions reactively altered by JOLs? (Psychon Bull Rev)
finding: Making JOLs does not reliably change what people choose to restudy. This argues against a 'changed goal' account of reactivity and favours a dual-task account.
numbers: Exp 1a N=140; Exp 1b N=202. BF10=0.46 and 0.22 (no JOL effect on restudy). JOLs related vs unrelated 69.44 vs 25.28 (d=2.89). Negative reactivity on recall of unrelated pairs b=-0.64.
limits: Restudy choices were not consequential. Relatedness is so strong it may mask subtle effects.
agent_relevance: Judgment can hurt performance through load rather than changed intent: keep judgment steps light.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large LMs are well calibrated on lettered multiple choice and true/false. Calibration improves with size and few-shot prompts. Models can judge P(True) of their own samples and be trained to predict P(IK), 'I know', before answering.
numbers: Models 800M-52B parameters. P(IK) trained on TriviaQA discriminates on math, Lambada and code, but is poorly calibrated out of distribution. 'None of the above' option reduces accuracy and calibration. RLHF policies look miscalibrated until temperature is tuned.
quote: Models perform well at predicting P(IK) and partially generalize across tasks, though they struggle with calibration of P(IK) on new tasks.
limits: Base models, not modern chat agents. P(IK) generalises only partially. Self-evaluation is harder because models find their own samples plausible.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a before-answer 'will I get this right' signal exists and can be read out (S0 gate), but must be trained or checked per domain.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) P(IK) responds to hints and sources
finding: P(IK) rises when relevant source text or a correct hint is in the prompt, and responds to incorrect or distracting hints too.
numbers: Sections 5.3-5.4 (TriviaQA sources, GSM8k hints). Two models of similar capability predict their own P(IK) somewhat better than the other model's.
limits: Exact increments are in figures I did not transcribe.
agent_relevance: The estimate behaves like a feeling of knowing that tracks available help, not only item wording.

source: Lin, Hilton & Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: A GPT-3 model fine-tuned to state confidence in words ('90% confidence') was calibrated in distribution and moderately calibrated under distribution shift. It was not just copying logits.
numbers: Introduces CalibratedMath. Both verbalized probability and logit-based uncertainty generalise calibration under shift (abstract and introduction read; tables not transcribed).
limits: Needs fine-tuning. Arithmetic domain.
agent_relevance: Verbalised confidence can be learned; it needs a training signal.

source: Yin et al. (2023) Do Large Language Models Know What They Don't Know? (SelfAware)
finding: Across 20 LLMs, models show some self-knowledge of unanswerable questions, which improves with in-context examples and instruction tuning. A gap to humans remains.
numbers: Best reported model F1 75.47% vs human 84.93% on the SelfAware set of unanswerable vs answerable questions.
quote: highlight a considerable gap between the capabilities of these models and human proficiency
limits: Unanswerable questions are categorical (no consensus, subjective); this is not the same as item-level 'will I recall this'.
agent_relevance: Detecting unanswerable tasks is possible but below human level, so the gate should not trust a bare self-report.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (ICLR)
finding: Verbalised confidence from black-box LLMs is overconfident and bunches at 80-100%. Human-inspired prompts and multi-sample consistency cut calibration error, but failure prediction stays weak.
numbers: Five LLMs, eight tasks. GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna mean ECE above 0.377. GPT-4 average AUROC about 62.7% (chance 50). White-box vs black-box gap narrow: AUROC 0.522 to 0.605. About 22.2% AUROC improvement from GPT-3 to GPT-4.
quote: LLMs tend to be highly overconfident when verbalizing their confidence
limits: Weak on professional-knowledge tasks. No strategy wins consistently; Self-Probing best on GPT-4, Top-K on GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: Verbal confidence from the agent itself is a weak failure detector. Use sampling agreement as a cross-check.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: For RLHF models, verbalised confidences are often better calibrated than token probabilities. Asking for several answers with probabilities helps (a 'consider the opposite' move).
numbers: Table 1 gpt-3.5-turbo, TriviaQA: label prob ECE 0.140, AUC 0.869; verbalized 1S top-4 ECE 0.054, AUC 0.896. TruthfulQA: label prob AUC 0.418 (below chance) vs verbal top-2 0.485. Abstract: ECE often cut by over 50%.
limits: TruthfulQA stays hard (all AUC under 0.65 for gpt-3.5). Model versions from mid-2023.
agent_relevance: Opposite emphasis to Xiong: prompt design decides whether verbal confidence works. Test each prompt on our own tasks.

source: Tian et al. (2023) GPT-4 table
finding: GPT-4 verbalised probabilities are better calibrated than its model probabilities. Calibration is much weaker on adversarial data than on factual recall.
numbers: GPT-4 TriviaQA: label prob ECE 0.078, AUC 0.950; verbal 1S top-1 ECE 0.024, AUC 0.937. TruthfulQA verbal 1S top-1 AUC 0.622.
limits: Table 2 caption says GPT-4 verbalised is substantially better calibrated.
agent_relevance: Calibration is domain-dependent. A single global trust number is unsafe.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What LLMs know and what people think they know (arXiv v2)
finding: Users trusted default LLM answers too much (calibration gap) and could not tell right from wrong answers (discrimination gap). Longer explanations raised confidence without raising accuracy. Matching explanation wording to model confidence narrowed both gaps.
numbers: Model confidence AUC .751 (GPT-3.5), .746 (PaLM2), .781 (GPT-4o short answer). Human AUC with default explanations .589, .602, .592. LLM accuracy 55% GPT-3.5 and 50% PaLM2 on 350 questions.
limits: Crowd participants, not experts. LLM overconfident on multiple choice and somewhat underconfident on short answer.
agent_relevance: If the agent reports confidence to a user, wording and length move the user's trust more than accuracy does.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
finding: Prompting alone does not give good uncertainty. Fine-tuning on about 1000 graded examples beats prompting baselines in ECE and AUROC. Models can estimate the uncertainty of other models.
numbers: 1000 graded examples enough with LoRA. Out-of-the-box ECE does not improve as the base model improves; AUROC improves slightly. User study N=181 (20 per variant).
limits: Needs open weights for the best method. One run takes 1-3 GPU days.
agent_relevance: A trained correctness probe is the stronger gate. Prompting a self-rating is the cheap fallback.

source: Huff & Ulakci (2025) Judgments of learning distinguish humans from LLMs in predicting memory (Sci Rep)
finding: Human JOLs predicted human recognition memory for garden-path sentences. GPT-3.5, GPT-4-turbo and GPT-4o JOLs did not.
numbers: Humans N=78 analysed (109 recruited), 45 sentences. Human slope: fitting B=0.167 [0.018,0.316]; unfitting B=0.104. All LLM slope CIs include zero (GPT-4o B=0.045 fitting, 0.027 unfitting). 100 samples per pair at temperature 1.
quote: none of the GPT models could predict human memory performance accurately across contexts
limits: Zero-shot only. Predicting human memory is a different target than predicting the model's own success. Samples treated as independent.
agent_relevance: Do not use an LLM as a proxy for how hard something is for a human. Use the agent's own outcomes as the criterion.

source: Synthesis: human delayed JOL vs LLM verbal confidence (from b01, b06, b19, b22)
finding: Humans and LLMs both show a good confidence-correctness link only under certain conditions. In humans it needs an unaided retrieval attempt; in LLMs it needs a prompt format that elicits alternatives or sampling.
numbers: Human cue-only delayed JOL: g=0.03 vs cue-target g=0.70 (as cited). LLM: Tian verbal ECE cut by over 50%; Xiong GPT-4 AUROC 62.7%.
limits: Synthesis of items read here; not a new measurement.
agent_relevance: Design rule: obtain confidence after a trial attempt (probe), from several samples, rather than from one cold rating.

source: Hart (1965) Memory and the feeling-of-knowing experience (founding study, not opened)
finding: Founding FOK study: people who fail to recall can predict later recognition above chance.
numbers: No numbers read this session.
limits: Not opened. Treat as unverified here.
agent_relevance: The original basis for the post-failure gate.

source: Evidence gap note: no FOK accuracy meta-analysis or large replication of Hart (1965) located
finding: Search quota ran out and API lookups were rate-limited (HTTP 429), so FOK meta-analyses and large replications were not found.
numbers: Zero sources for a FOK accuracy meta-analysis.
limits: Gap in this file. Another pass should look for Schwartz, Koriat and Metcalfe FOK reviews.
agent_relevance: Do not treat FOK strength as established beyond the items listed here.
